The CHA2DS2-VASc scoring system is utilized across [[danmark|Danmark]] healthcare regions to assess stroke risk, though its application and the resulting score distributions vary significantly depending on the specific patient population being analyzed. This comparison examines regional data from two distinct cohorts: patients who suffered an intracranial hemorrhage and incident patients with [[atrieflimren]] (atrial fibrillation).

For patients with intracranial hemorrhage, the national cohort comprised 711 individuals, with the majority falling into the lower-to-moderate risk categories [^src1]. [[region-hovedstaden|Region Hovedstaden]] recorded the highest proportion of patients with a score of 1, accounting for 40.7% of its regional cohort [^src1]. Conversely, [[region-sjaelland|Region Sjælland]] and [[region-nordjylland|Region Nordjylland]] tied for the lowest proportion of patients with a score of 0, both at 6.8% [^src1]. Notably, Region Sjælland stood out as an outlier in the higher risk categories, presenting the highest regional percentage of patients with a score of 4 at 8.7%, well above the national average of 4.8% [^src1].

In contrast, the data for incident atrial fibrillation patients encompasses a much larger national cohort of 22,073 individuals [^src2]. Across all regions, the median CHA2DS2-VASc score remained uniformly constant at 2.00 [^src2]. However, the mean scores revealed slight regional variations, with Region Sjælland exhibiting the highest average score of 1.81, while Region Hovedstaden, [[region-midtjylland|Region Midtjylland]], and Region Nordjylland shared the lowest mean of 1.73 [^src2]. Furthermore, while the maximum recorded score reached 6.00 in Danmark overall, as well as in Region Hovedstaden, [[region-syddanmark|Region Syddanmark]], and Region Midtjylland, the maximum score was capped at 5.00 in both Region Sjælland and Region Nordjylland [^src2].

Because the two datasets evaluate different clinical populations—intracranial hemorrhage patients versus incident atrial fibrillation patients—and employ different statistical presentations (categorical percentages versus descriptive statistics), a direct temporal trend cannot be established between the two reports. Instead, the data highlights how baseline risk profiles differ fundamentally across distinct cardiovascular and neurological events within the same regional healthcare structures.
